[RESPONSE] The patient's chief complaint is difficulty combing his hair and difficulty reaching objects on high shelves, both for the past few months.

[THOUGHT] The pattern (difficulty combing hair, reaching high shelves) suggests proximal shoulder girdle weakness. Determining whether weakness is bilateral and symmetric will narrow differential (inflammatory myopathy, muscular dystrophy, endocrine myopathy vs focal rotator cuff/nerve lesions). I need that specific detail before ordering tests.

[QUERY] Is the weakness affecting both arms symmetrically, or is it worse on one side?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure; I can't recall whether it's worse on one side or affecting both arms equally.

[THOUGHT] Age and sex influence the differential for proximal weakness (e.g., polymyositis/dermatomyositis in adults, limb-girdle dystrophy in younger, inclusion body myositis in older males). I need this basic demographic before ordering specific tests.

[QUERY] What is the patient's age and sex?

[REFERENCE] 1. 65-year-old male

[RESPONSE] He is a 65-year-old male.

[THOUGHT] Proximal upper-limb weakness in a 65-year-old man raises inclusion body myositis, polymyositis, or other myopathies. Distal or lower-limb involvement (difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs) and presence of dysphagia would strongly point toward IBM or another inflammatory myopathy. I need to know about lower-limb proximal weakness next.

[QUERY] Has he had any difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, or standing up from a low seat?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall having trouble rising from a chair, climbing stairs, or standing up from a low seat.

[THOUGHT] Dysphagia is common in inclusion body myositis and inflammatory myopathies and would help distinguish IBM (often has prominent dysphagia) from other causes. Asking about swallowing difficulty is a single, specific question that closes a key information gap.

[QUERY] Has he had any difficulty swallowing, choking, or coughing when eating solids or liquids (dysphagia) or noticed food sticking in his throat?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall having any difficulty swallowing, choking, or coughing when eating.

[THOUGHT] Inclusion body myositis often causes finger flexor weakness and difficulty with fine hand tasks in older men, which helps distinguish it from polymyositis/dermatomyositis. I need to know about distal hand function before ordering labs.

[QUERY] Does he have any difficulty with fine hand tasks—buttoning shirts, turning keys, opening jars, or a weak grip?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure; I don't recall any information about difficulty with fine hand tasks like buttoning shirts, turning keys, opening jars, or a weak grip.

[THOUGHT] In a 65-year-old man with proximal shoulder girdle weakness, distinguishing inclusion body myositis (often causes finger flexor weakness and weak grip) from other myopathies is critical. The patient was unsure about fine hand tasks earlier, so I must ask one specific question targeting finger flexor/grip weakness to help support or refute IBM.

[QUERY] Does he have difficulty making a fist or a noticeably weak grip (trouble holding a cup or opening jars) specifically due to finger/hand weakness?

[REFERENCE] 9. No fever, weight loss, or other joint involvement.

[RESPONSE] No — he does not have other joint involvement, so he does not report difficulty making a fist or a noticeably weak grip from finger/hand weakness.

[THOUGHT] The leading possibilities are inflammatory myopathy (polymyositis), statin or endocrine myopathy, or less likely inclusion body myositis given absent dysphagia and hand weakness. A serum creatine kinase (CK) will quickly indicate muscle injury and help distinguish myopathic from neurogenic causes and guide further testing (ESR/CRP, TSH, EMG, biopsy). I'll request CK first.

[TEST] Order serum creatine kinase (CK) level.
Normal

[THOUGHT] A normal CK makes inflammatory myopathy less likely but doesn't exclude it. Distinguishing true muscle weakness from pain- or stiffness-limited shoulder motion is essential to narrow causes (rotator cuff/shoulder pathology vs myopathy). I should first ask about pain with shoulder movement.

[QUERY] Does he have shoulder pain or stiffness when lifting his arms or reaching overhead?

[REFERENCE] 3. The patient reports difficulty reaching objects on high shelves for the past few months.
[REFERENCE] 4. Stiffness in the arm

[RESPONSE] Yes. He reports difficulty reaching objects on high shelves for the past few months and has stiffness in the arm.

[THOUGHT] Passive shoulder motion being limited suggests adhesive capsulitis ("frozen shoulder"); preserved passive motion with limited active motion suggests rotator cuff tear/tendinopathy. This question will distinguish those and guide imaging versus EMG/labs.

[QUERY] When someone else moves his affected shoulder (passive motion), is the range of motion limited or painful, or is it relatively preserved?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall whether someone else moving my shoulder causes pain or limits the range of motion.

[THOUGHT] Night pain is common with rotator cuff tendinopathy/tear and can help distinguish rotator cuff pathology from other causes; asking about nocturnal pain is a single, specific item that fills a key gap.

[QUERY] Do you have significant shoulder pain at night that wakes you or prevents you from sleeping on that side?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall having significant shoulder pain at night that wakes me or prevents me from sleeping on that side.

[THOUGHT] Distinguishing adhesive capsulitis (limited passive and active ROM) from rotator cuff tear/tendinopathy (preserved passive ROM, weak abduction/external rotation, positive impingement/drop-arm) will direct diagnosis. A focused shoulder exam comparing active vs passive range of motion and rotator cuff strength/impingement signs is the single most informative next step.

[TEST] Perform a focused bilateral shoulder examination: document active and passive range of motion, abduction and external rotation strength, and check for painful arc, impingement signs (Neer/Hawkins), and drop-arm sign.

[THOUGHT] Decreased passive and active shoulder ROM with tenderness and mildly reduced strength points strongly to adhesive capsulitis. Diabetes is a major risk factor and would support this diagnosis. I need that single comorbidity detail to strengthen the likelihood before finalizing the diagnosis.

[QUERY] Does he have a history of diabetes mellitus?

[REFERENCE] 5. Diabetes mellitus type II, obesity, hypertension.
[RESPONSE] Yes. He has diabetes mellitus type II.

[THOUGHT] This patient's progressive difficulty reaching overhead with stiffness, tenderness, and both decreased active and passive shoulder range of motion, normal rotator cuff tests (painful arc, impingement, drop-arm), normal CK, and a history of type 2 diabetes strongly support adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder). The combination of limited passive motion (key distinguishing feature from rotator cuff tear or myopathy) plus diabetes (a major risk factor) makes adhesive capsulitis the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder).
